## Today's mission {.big .center}

::: {.big .center}
Make your research easier to re-run, understand and share.
:::

::: notes
Works for R, Python and spreadsheet users. Demo in Positron, but everything can be done in any IDE or the terminal. The notes are a reference for afterwards; the slides and demos carry the session.
:::

## How today works

::: {.medium}
Do it together. Then try it yourself.
:::

::: {.small}
- Each topic is **one short activity**: we do a part together, you try something on your own, then I show the answer
- The activities **don't need you to run any code**: the only thing we run is **Render**
- Everything you need is in the **example folder**
- Stuck? **Type in the chat**
:::

# [01]{.section-number} Project structures {.section-divider background-color="var(--jgi-red)"}

[How should I organise a project so I, and others, can find things and re-run them?]{.section-question}

## Why bother?

::: {.cards .grid2}
::: {.card .fragment}
**Future you**
Code written as if others will use it is easier to return to after a holiday, or in six months' time
:::
::: {.card .fragment}
**Speed**
A project set up as a pipeline can be re-run quickly when the data changes or a reviewer asks for something new
:::
::: {.card .fragment}
**Confidence**
You understand how the pieces fit together, and where things might go wrong
:::
::: {.card .fragment}
**Sharing and careers**
Journals and funders increasingly expect shared code and data, and tidy work is easy to trust
:::
:::

::: notes
Selfish reasons first: this mostly helps you. Mention the three problems with a messy project: hard to maintain, hard to run somewhere else, hard to understand.
:::

## Think about pipelines

::: {.flow}
[Raw data]{.step} [→]{.arrow} [Clean]{.step} [→]{.arrow} [Analyse]{.step} [→]{.arrow} [Results]{.step}
:::

- Never overwrite the raw data
- Everything after it can be re-made by running the code
- So the raw data and the code are what you must protect

::: notes
Spreadsheet users: same idea. Raw file untouched, a working copy, one named sheet per step, and a README describing each step.
:::

```{.md}
clean.R                   results.xlsx
data.csv                  results_v3.xlsx
data_FINAL_USE_THIS.csv   untitled.R
data_final.csv
data_final_v2.csv
```

::: {.cards}
::: {.card}
**1**

Which file is the **raw data**?
:::
::: {.card}
**2**

What do I **run first**?
:::
::: {.card}
**3**

Which figure came from which analysis?
:::
:::

Together, 4 min. Put up the file list and ask the three questions. Ask people to type their answers in the chat, and let everyone feel the problem: it is nobody's fault, this happens naturally. Open `notes.txt` and one of the scripts from the example folder if you like (absolute paths, packages with no versions). Then move to the next slide.
:::

:::

Your turn, 6 min, on their own, on paper or in a document. No code. The course is online, so there is no pair work: ask people to post one surprising file or decision in the chat at the end. There is no single right answer: they are deciding what each file is for.

## What goes where {.demo-slide}

[Answer]{.answer-tag} [4 min]{.demo-meta}

::: {.doc-table}

| | Files | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| **Raw data** | `data.csv` | Never edit it |
| **Cleaned data** | `data_final.csv`, `data_final_v2.csv`, `data_FINAL_USE_THIS.csv` | Three versions of one thing: make it from the raw data with code |
| **Code** | `clean.R`, `analysis.R`, `analysis2 (copy).R`, `analysis_OLD.R`, `untitled.R` | One script per step, numbered. Delete the copies |
| **Results** | `plot1.png`, `plot_new.png`, `results.xlsx`, `results_v3.xlsx` | The code can re-make these |
| **Documents** | `notes.txt`, `report_draft.docx` | Become the README and the report |
| **Delete** | `Copy of data.csv` | A duplicate |

:::

::: notes
Answer, part one. Go through the table row by row. Ask who disagreed, and why. The key point is the first row and the "cleaned data" row: three versions of the same thing, with no way to tell which is right.
:::

## The tidy version {.demo-slide}

[Answer]{.answer-tag} [2 min]{.demo-meta}

```
tidy-project/
├── README.md                          how to run it
├── report.qmd                         the report
├── _quarto.yml                        report settings
├── data/
│   ├── raw/penguins.csv               never edited
│   └── processed/
│       ├── penguins_clean.csv         made by the code
│       └── penguins_clean_dictionary.csv   explains each column
├── code/
│   ├── 01_clean_data.R                numbered, in order
│   └── run_all.R                      rebuilds everything
└── outputs/                           made by the code: safe to delete
```

::: notes
Answer, part two. This is the project you rebuilt in the demo. Point out that it is the same data, just organised. The README and the data dictionary come next.
:::

# [02]{.section-number} Documentation & Quarto {.section-divider background-color="var(--jgi-red)"}

[How do I explain my project, and report on it, so others (and future me) can use it?]{.section-question}

## Four kinds of documentation

::: {.doc-table}

| | Comments in code | Files in the repo | Data dictionary | External documentation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Where** | Scripts and notebooks | `README.md` | A CSV next to the data | A website or report |
| **Why** | Explain *why*, not what | How to use the project | What each column means | What you did, in plain terms |
| **Who for** | Other researchers | People running your code | Anyone using the data | Less technical readers |
| **Example** | `# outliers removed, as agreed with the lab` | Quickstart and setup | `bill_len`: bill length, in mm | A Quarto report |

:::

<br>

::: {.muted .center}
Write for the person who will read it, which includes yourself!
:::

::: notes
Go through the four in turn, and ask who they are writing for. Comments are for people reading the code, the README is for people running it, the data dictionary is for people using the data, and external documentation is for people who may never see the code. The rest of this section covers the README, the data dictionary and reports written in Quarto.
:::

## What goes in a README?

- **Summary** and status
- **Quickstart**: which files, in what order
- **Setup**: what to install first
- **Contents**: what each folder holds

::: {.good}
✔ No code? A README is still the best way to document your project
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Using AI
Be careful getting an LLM to create your README. While it can save time, you may inadvertently upload all your data and results by giving access to your folders! Instead, draft one yourself and then use a chatbot to help refine it!
:::

::: notes
Show a real README. Point out it is just a text file written in Markdown. The next activity is about what makes one useful.
:::

## The README {.demo-slide}

[Answer]{.answer-tag} [2 min]{.demo-meta}

````markdown
# Penguin body mass analysis

Body measurements of 333 penguins on three islands. **Status:** complete.

## Quickstart
1. Open this folder in RStudio or Positron
2. Run `code/run_all.R`

## Setup
- R 4.3 or later
- Quarto 1.4 or later

## Contents
- `data/raw/` the original data (never edited)
- `data/processed/` cleaned data, and a data dictionary
- `code/` the scripts
- `report.qmd` the report
````

::: notes
Answer, part one: the README from `tidy-project`. It answers all three questions: how to run it, what software, what is where. The next slide shows the data dictionary, which answers the column question.
:::

## The data dictionary {.demo-slide}

[Answer]{.answer-tag} [2 min]{.demo-meta}

| column | type | description | units / values |
|---|---|---|---|
| `species` | text | Penguin species | Adelie, Chinstrap, Gentoo |
| `bill_len` | number | Bill length | mm |
| `body_mass` | number | Body mass | grams |
| `sex` | text | Sex of the penguin | female, male; blank if not recorded |

::: notes
Answer, part two. The dictionary has one row per column: what it is, its type and its units. Copying the column names is the easy part. The descriptions are the value, and only the person who knows the data can write them.
:::

## What is Quarto?

::: {.small}
- Write **text and code in one file**
- **Render** it into a report: HTML, PDF or Word
- The results **come from the code**
- Free and open source: [quarto.org](https://quarto.org)
:::

::: {.flow}
[report.qmd]{.step .fragment} [→]{.arrow .fragment} [HTML]{.step .light .fragment} [PDF]{.step .light .fragment} [Word]{.step .light .fragment}
:::

::: notes
Quarto is the tool this whole course is built with: the slides, the notes and the website are all Quarto. It is free, and works with R, Python and Julia.
:::

## Why Quarto for reproducible research?

::: {.cards .grid2}
::: {.card}
**No copy and paste**
Numbers, tables and figures come straight from the code, so they can't drift out of sync with the analysis
:::
::: {.card}
**Always up to date**
If the data changes, render again and the whole report updates
:::
::: {.card}
**One source, many outputs**
The same file can make HTML, PDF, Word, slides and websites
:::
::: {.card}
**Plain text**
Easy to share, compare and keep in version control, in any editor
:::
:::

::: notes
The key idea is that the report *is* the analysis. A reader, or you in six months, can see exactly how every number was produced, and re-create it.
:::

## The old way vs the Quarto way

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Without Quarto**

::: {.bad}
1. Run the analysis
2. Copy numbers and plots into a Word document
3. The data changes
4. Repeat by hand, and hope you caught every number
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**With Quarto**

::: {.good}
1. Write the report once, with the code in it
2. Render
3. The data changes
4. Render again
:::
:::
::::

## Weaving text and analysis together

````markdown
---
title: "Penguin report"
format: html
author: Josh Tyler
---

## Data

```{{r}}
clean <- read.csv("data/processed/penguins_clean.csv")
```

There are `{{r}} nrow(clean)` penguins in the data.
````

::: notes
In a real file the header sits between two lines of three dashes. Next slide: the four parts.
:::

## The four parts of a Quarto file

::: {.cards .grid2}
::: {.card}
**1 · Header**

The title and the output format
:::
::: {.card}
**2 · Text**

Ordinary Markdown, with headings and lists
:::
::: {.card}
**3 · Code chunk**

The code runs when you render, and its output appears underneath
:::
::: {.card}
**4 · Inline code**

A result inside a sentence, recalculated every time
:::
:::

::: notes
Point at each part on the previous slide. Inline code is the clever bit: the number in the sentence is calculated every time the report is rendered.
:::

## If the data changes, the report updates

::: {.flow}
[New data]{.step} [→]{.arrow} [Re-run the code & Render]{.step} [→]{.arrow} [Updated report]{.step}
:::

::: {.small}
- Every number, table and figure is recalculated
- Sentences with inline code update too
- There is nothing to copy and paste
:::

::: {.good}
✔ Change the data (or the code), not the report
:::

# [03]{.section-number} Virtual environments {.section-divider background-color="var(--jgi-red)"}

[How do I make sure my code still runs next month, or on someone else's computer?]{.section-question}

## The problem: "it worked last year"

1. Last year: your analysis runs, using version 1.2 of a package
2. This year: a new project needs version 1.3, so you update
3. You re-run last year's analysis: **it breaks**, or gives different results 💥

::: {.muted}
Your computer has one shared set of packages, so two projects that need different versions can't both be happy
:::

::: notes
Everyone who has coded for a while has had this. The same code, a different version of a package, and a different result, or an error. Ask who has had it.
:::

## Why does this happen?

::: {.cards .grid2}
::: {.card}
**Packages change**
Functions are renamed, defaults change and bugs are fixed
:::
::: {.card}
**Your code depends on them**
The same code with a different package version can give a different result
:::
::: {.card}
**Other computers differ**
A colleague, a new laptop or an HPC: "it works on my machine"
:::
::: {.card}
**Nothing records it**
Your project doesn't say which versions it needs, so nobody can tell what went wrong
:::
:::

## What is an environment?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Without environments**

::: {.bad}
One shared library of packages for every project on your computer
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**With environments**

::: {.good}
Each project has its own set of packages, at the versions it needs
:::
:::
::::

::: {.flow}
[Project 1]{.step} [→]{.arrow} [package v1.2]{.step .light}
:::
::: {.flow}
[Project 2]{.step} [→]{.arrow} [package v1.3]{.step .light}
:::

::: notes
An environment is a project's own folder of installed packages. Projects can no longer interfere with each other, and each one has what it needs.
:::

## How do environments work?

::: {.flow .small}
[Lock file]{.step} [→]{.arrow} [Create the environment]{.step} [→]{.arrow} [Packages installed]{.step}
:::

::: {.small}
- The **lock file** is the recipe: an exact list of packages and versions. It is small, and you keep it with your project
- The **environment** is what gets built from it: the installed packages, in their own folder
- Your code only sees the packages in **its own** environment
- The environment is **disposable**: delete it, and rebuild it from the lock file whenever you like
:::

## The tools

::: {.doc-table .big}

| | Python | R |
|---|---|---|
| **Tool** | `uv` | `renv` |
| **Lock file** (keep it) | `uv.lock` | `renv.lock` |
| **Environment** (disposable) | `.venv` | `renv/library` |
| **Rebuild it** | `uv sync` | `renv::restore()` |

:::

::: notes
Other tools do the same job: conda and pixi (which can install Python, R and other software in one environment), and Python's built-in venv. The idea is the same whichever you use: a file that records what the project needs. Point out that the notes (section 3.2) have a fuller table with conda and pixi in it.
:::

## Send your project to someone, and it works

::: {.flow .small}
[Your project +<br>lock file]{.step} [→]{.arrow} [Colleague rebuilds<br>the environment]{.step} [→]{.arrow} [Same packages,<br>same results]{.step}
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.good}
✔ **Send:** your code, README and lock file (and the data, if you can)
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.bad}
✘ **Don't send:** the environment itself. It is large, and specific to your computer
:::
:::
::::

::: notes
This is the payoff. The lock file travels with the project, by email, zip or git. Your colleague, a reviewer, or you on a new laptop runs one command and gets the same packages. You can send it to a reviewer and it will run first time.
:::

## What environments don't cover

::: {.small}
- They record **packages**. Also write down the version of **R or Python** in your README (`uv` can pin Python; `renv` records the R version but doesn't install it)
- The **operating system** and hardware can still differ
- They don't include your **data**
:::

::: {.muted}
Good enough for almost every project. Perfect is not the goal!
:::

## No code? Record it anyway

::: {.good}
✔ Write the program, its version and any add-ins in your README: the next person then knows what you used
:::

## Live demo: delete it, then rebuild it {.demo-slide}

[Live demo]{.demo-tag} [5 min]{.demo-meta}

::: {.medium}
1. Here is a project's environment
2. Delete it
3. Rebuild it from the lock file: one command
:::

::: notes
STOP HERE and switch to the demo. R: in a copy of `environment-demo/r` from the example folder, run `renv::init()`, then `source("code/analysis.R")`. Close the project, delete `renv/library`, open it again (ggplot2 is now missing) and run `renv::restore()`. Python: in a copy of `environment-demo/python` from the example folder, run `uv init --no-package`, then `uv add pandas matplotlib`, then `uv run code/analysis.py`. Delete `.venv` and run `uv sync` to rebuild it (the steps are in its README). Say: "this is what your colleague does when you send them the project". Note that renv records package versions but not the version of R itself. If you have no environment ready, show the lock file in `environment-demo/r/finished/` or `environment-demo/python/finished/` and describe it instead. If it fails, say so and move on: this is a watch-only demo.
:::

::: notes
Your turn, 6 min, on their own. No code. Resist giving hints: let them find the list. At the end, ask people to type their list in the chat, and read out a few.
:::

## The new laptop test {.demo-slide}

[Answer]{.answer-tag} [3 min]{.demo-meta}

::: {.doc-table}

| You need to know | Where it should be written down |
|---|---|
| Which **software**, and which version | The README (Setup) |
| Which **packages**, and which versions | A lock file |
| Where the **data** is | The README, and a `data/raw` folder |
| **What to run**, and in what order | The README (Quickstart), or one script |
| Where the **results** come from | The code, not copy and paste |

:::

::: notes
Answer. Compare their lists with the table. Almost everything on it can be written down once in a README, and a lock file does the packages automatically. This is exactly what `tidy-project/README.md` does.
:::

# [04]{.section-number} Your first step {.section-divider background-color="var(--jgi-red)"}

[What will you do differently on Monday?]{.section-question}

## From messy to shareable {.demo-slide}

[Together]{.demo-tag} [3 min]{.demo-meta}

::: {.flow}
[Messy]{.step .light} [→]{.arrow} [Tidy]{.step} [→]{.arrow} [Documented]{.step} <br> [→]{.arrow} [Reported]{.step} [→]{.arrow} [Recorded]{.step} [→]{.arrow} [Shareable]{.step}
:::

::: {.small}
- **Tidy:** raw data kept apart and never edited
- **Documented:** a README and a data dictionary
- **Reported:** one document, made from the data and code
- **Recorded:** the software and versions written down
- **Shareable:** a project a colleague can run on a new computer
:::

::: notes
Together, 3 min. This is the whole course on one slide. Every step is a habit, and you can start with any of them.
:::

☐ Raw data never edited

::: {.card}

Your turn, 6 min. They tick the checklist for a project of their own (or the messy one if they have none). Then circle ONE thing, and post it in the chat. The printable checklist is in the example folder (`checklist.pdf` and `checklist.docx`).
:::

## Quick wins {.demo-slide}

[Answer]{.answer-tag} [3 min]{.demo-meta}

<br>

::: {.doc-table .medium}

| Quick win | Time | Why it helps |
|---|---|---|
| Stop editing the raw data | 0 min | Everything can be re-made |
| Clear folders and file names | 15 min | You can find things |
| Write a README | 15 min | Others, and future you, can run it |
| Write down your software versions | 5 min | It runs on another computer |
| Describe your columns | 20 min | Your data makes sense to others |

:::

::: notes
Answer, 3 min. The biggest wins for the least effort are at the top. Encourage everyone to start with the first thing they circled, or the one at the top of this list.
:::

# [★]{.section-number} Optional: if there is time {.section-divider background-color="var(--jgi-red)"}

[Sharing your data: Q-FAIR]{.section-question}

::: notes
These slides are optional. Use them if there is time, and skip them if not. The notes cover Q-FAIR in full.
:::

## Q-FAIR data principles

::: {.cards}
::: {.card}
**Q**uality
Accurate, complete, documented
:::
::: {.card}
**F**indable
Clear names and description
:::
::: {.card}
**A**ccessible
Clear how to get it
:::
::: {.card}
**I**nteroperable
Open, standard formats
:::
::: {.card}
**R**eusable
Documented, with a licence
:::
:::

::: {.small}
Read more: [the FAIR principles](https://www.go-fair.org/fair-principles/)
:::

::: notes
Link Q, F and A back to earlier sections (read-only raw data, README, setup notes). The next slides cover I and R. Keep this section brisk: it is a signpost, not a tutorial.
:::

## Why it matters

::: {.small}
- **Funders and journals** increasingly expect data to be shared
- **Others can build on your work**, and check it
- **Future you** can find and understand your own data
- Your work **gets cited**
:::

::: notes
Quality comes first: there is no point sharing data that nobody can trust or understand.
:::

## Four things to do

::: {.doc-table}

| | What to do | Learn more |
|---|---|---|
| **Open formats** | Share data as CSV, not a format that needs one program | [Turing Way: research data management](https://book.the-turing-way.org/reproducible-research/rdm) |
| **Describe it** | Write a data dictionary: what each column means, its units and missing values | See section 2 |
| **Add a licence** | Data: CC BY 4.0. Code: MIT | [Creative Commons chooser](https://creativecommons.org/chooser/), [choosealicense.com](https://choosealicense.com) |
| **Deposit it** | A repository that gives a DOI, such as Zenodo or your institution's | [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org) |

:::

::: {.muted .center}
Can't share the data? Share the README and data dictionary, and explain how to ask for access
:::

::: notes
Open formats: in Excel use File > Save As > CSV UTF-8, one sheet per file, and note that formulas become values. A data dictionary has one row per column, as in section 2. Check funder and institution requirements for licences. Refer ethics and consent questions to the research data team.
:::

[Your turn]{.your-turn-tag} [4 min]{.demo-meta}

::: {.card}
**A**

:::
::: {.card}
**B**
A CSV in a repository, with a DOI, a README, a data dictionary and a CC BY licence.
:::
::: {.card}
**C**
A CSV on the department shared drive, with a README. No licence, and you need to ask the group's admin for access.
:::
:::

::: {.small}
For each one, mark every letter of **Q-FAIR** with a ✔ or an ✘.
:::

## Q-FAIR detective {.demo-slide}

[Answer]{.answer-tag} [2 min]{.demo-meta}

::: {.doc-table}

| | **Q** | **F** | **A** | **I** | **R** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A** The spreadsheet | ✘ | ✘ | ✘ | ✘ | ✘ |
| **B** The repository CSV | ✔ | ✔ | ✔ | ✔ | ✔ |
| **C** The shared-drive CSV | ✔ | ✘ | partly | ✔ | ✘ |

:::

::: {.small}
**C** is documented (Q) and in an open format (I), but hard to find (F), needs permission (A), and has no licence (R).
:::
